messages.subject_clean: Age estimation using hierarchical ordinal logistic model
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Being a inexperimented modeller, I would like to ask a review of my analysis.

I am trying to estimate the age of some animals based on their teeth status. I thought to use the ordinal logistic model described in Jackman 2009, p: 410.
https://books.google.ch/books?id=QFqyrNL8yEkC&printsec=frontcover&dq=Bayesian+analysis+for+the+social+sciences&hl=fr&sa=X&ei=eBH4VPj1DIThONySgdgB&ved=0CB0Q6AEwAA#v=onepage&q=Bayesian%20analysis%20for%20the%20social%20sciences&f=false

In the populations we study, we can know the age of the animals only when they are juvenile or immature. Otherwise, we report the teeth abrasion status (7 levels). Thus we can work with 9 different age levels. With recapture, we can use the time since the first capture as the explanatory variable of the teeth abrasion. Like the interview example of Jackman 2009, I consider the age at the first capture like the interviewer heterogeneity. Indeed, the teeth of an old individual will be considered differently compared to the ones of a young one.

However, I am more interested in modelling the age before the first capture than correcting the individual heterogeneity. In that sense, I prefer to correct the independent variable, by adding an estimated correction (age before first manip) than the response variable. I am not sure if this is correct, because this variable is not random, as expected for such heterogeneity. We have more and more individuals with known age (close to 0) and this variable cannot be negative.

I have added the script and the txt file. Some improvements still to be done on the initialisation as the model need to be relaunch some times... The chains converged rapidly and the estimations are making sense. Could you please tell me if the mathematical background is ok.
#function to create data at initialisation for age before ringing
datasim <- function(data2){
    dataAge2sim <- array(NA,length(data2))
    for(i in 1:length(data2)){
        dataAge2sim[i] <- ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(data2[i]), runif(1,0,15),NA)}
return(dataAge2sim)}

sink("ms3.jags")
cat("
model {

    for(i in 1:N){  ## loop over observations
          ## form the linear predictor
          mu[i] <-(x[i]+before[id[i]])*lin

          ## cumulative logistic probabilities
          logit(Q[i,1]) <- tau[1]-mu[i]
          p[i,1] <- Q[i,1]
          for(j in 2:8){
                logit(Q[i,j]) <- tau[j]-mu[i]
                p[i,j] <- Q[i,j] - Q[i,j-1]
          }
          p[i,9] <- 1 - Q[i,8]
          y[i] ~ dcat(p[i,1:9])  ## p[i,] sums to 1 for each i
    }
    ## priors over lin parameter
    lin~ dnorm(0,0.0001)

    ## hierarchical model over known age
    for(k in 1:NID){
          before[k] ~ dnorm(0,eta.tau)}

    eta.tau <- 1/pow(sd,2)
    sd ~ dunif(0,3)

    ## priors over thresholds constraint to be ordered
        for(i in 1:7){
    tau0[i]~dunif(tau[1],15)}
    tau[2:8] <- sort(tau0)
    tau[1] <- tauJ*lin}

     ",fill = TRUE)
sink()
# Bundle data
jags.data <- list(NID=NID,x=data$age_after_firstmanip,y= data$age_Teeth,id=id,N=N,tauJ=tauJ,before= age_before_firstmanip)

# Initial values
inits <- function(){list(before=datasim(age_before_firstmanip),tau0 = runif(7,1,15),lin=rnorm(1),sd=runif(1,0,3)) }

# Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("before","lin", "sd","tau")

# MCMC settings
ni <- 5000
nt <- 3
nb <- 2000
nc <- 3

# Call JAGS from R
ms3 <- jags(jags.data, inits, parameters, "ms3.jags", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni,  n.burnin = nb, working.directory = getwd())

TauJ is the known age for the first threshold.

Thank you

messages.subject: Cross-validation in hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all!

I am currently using hierarchical models for modelling abundance (N-mixture
with distance sampling, Royle 2004 - the JAGS implementation of generalized
"gdistsamp-like" model - in terms of the unmarked package).

As the model will be used to predict abundance at sites where we don't have
any counts, I think cross-validation of the model is necessary (i.e. put
some data apart and test the model on them). I tried to take the Predictive
Posterior Checks suggested by Marc & Michael in BPA chapter 12.3.1 and generalized
them for cross-validation. I am however not sure about it and would like to
discuss this approach here.

It is not easy to post formulas and pictures in email so please follow my
full question here:

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/141005/crossvalidation-in-hierarchical-bayesian-models-hbms

you may also answer there if you want.

Thanks a lot!

Best regards,

        Tomas

P.S.: Marc, sorry for using the term "bayesian model" in the question... I agree with your opinion,
unfortunatelly HBM seems to be established term now... :-/

messages.subject: Nested Random Effects in BUGS/JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

It's straightforward to fit simple random effects in BUGS/JAGS, but I'm wondering how to go about fitting 'nested random effects', which are common and easy to implement in the various R packages for generalized linear mixed models. I'll use a classic toy example to outline a situation where a nested random effect would be preferred over a simple one (there are many ecological analogies).

Lets say you want to account for random variation in student test scores (students take multiple tests) but the students are nested within different classrooms. To make things realistic, lets also assume there are different numbers of students in each classroom.

In the R packages, one would specify the following to model random variation in intercept among students within classroom:

fixedeffects + (1|classroom:student)

Or, if one wants to model random variation in intercept among classrooms and among students within classrooms:

fixedeffects + (1|classroom/student)

[a helpful reference: https://www.nceas.ucsb.edu/system/files/mixed.pdf]

I’ve scoured several textbooks and online sources for examples of how to code nested random effects in the BUGS/JAGS language, but for the life of me, I can’t find examples…only unanswered posts. Does anyone have any suggestions, or even a source with an example?

Very grateful for your help,

Dave Koons

Hi All,

I'm trying to run a distance-sampling analysis using Bayesian methods, but I'm having trouble just getting the code to run at all. I'm using code very similar to Chelgren et al. 2011 and Shirk et al. 2014, except that I've tried to modify it to accommodate repeat sampling of the same transect.  I have about 1,000 total transects, and I collected data on some or all of these transects on 5 occasions. I assume that the population is open to demographic change between the sampling occasions, so I'm just trying to get 5 separate density estimates, one for each occasion.

When I run the code in WinBUGs, I get the error "undefined real result".  I googled this and it sounds like it can either be from poor initial values or numerically impossible values.  I'm extremely new to WinBUGs and Bayesian modeling, so I'm not at all sure if I'm providing the correct initial values and if there are other initial values that I should provide, or if this is the problem at all. My code is below, and I attached a screenshot of the error log; if anyone has any suggestions on things I should try that might get it to run, I would greatly appreciate it. And please let me know if I should provide more information.

Thank you!

Lucretia

#specifications for model
transects <- 1051 #number of transects
transects1 <- c(31,40,55,92,95) #number of transects in each survey occasion
    #that have greater than zero detections
n.patches <- 86 #number of territories within which transects are sampled
occasions <- 5 #number of sampling occasions, popn not demographically
    #closed between occasions

#import y data and convert 2D y matrix to 3D
#y data are the detection distances for each transect for each sampling occasion
#the dimensions are number of transects (1051) by max number of detections per tx (4)
#by number of sampling occasions (5)
ydat <- read.csv("y_8jan15.csv",header=T,sep=",")
y<- array(NA,c(1051,4, 5))#[n,i,k]
for (k in 1:5){
    sel.rows <- ydat$occasion==k
    y[,,k] <- as.matrix(ydat)[sel.rows,5:8]
    } #k
class(y) <- "numeric"
str(y)

#import n detections
#a count of the number of detections at each transect for each sampling occasion
ndat <- read.csv("n_8jan15.csv",header=T,sep=",")
n <- as.matrix(ndat[,3:7])

#vector of transect lengths
L <- ndat$length

#vector identifying which patch a transect is in
patch.id <http://patch.id> <- as.integer(factor(ndat$territory, unique(ndat$territory)))

#import matrix indexing transects with >=1 detection for each occasion
#this provides an index later so that the likelihood is not calculated over
#transects with no data
tran1_ik <- read.csv("tran1_detection_index.csv",header=T,sep=",")
tran1_ik <- as.matrix(tran1_ik)

#import transect level covariates
Xdat <- read.csv("X_tx_covs_8jan15.csv",header=T,sep=",")

#reduce X to a matrix of non-correlated covariates
X <- as.matrix(Xdat[,c(4,6,8,10,13,14,15,16,17,19)])
X <- scale(X)

#import patch level covariates
Zdat <- read.csv("Z_tx_covs_8jan15.csv",header=T,sep=",")

#reduce Z to a matrix of non-correlated covariates
Z <- as.matrix(Zdat[,c(4,5,7,9,12,13,14,15,16,18)])
Z <- scale(Z)

W <- 300 #strip width

T <- W  #truncation distance

#load OpenBugs or WinBugs package & directories
library(R2WinBUGS)
bugs.dir <- "D:/Lucretia/GIS_&_R_stuff/Bayesian_stats_class_Sep2014/Winbugs14/WinBUGS14"

#the model:
sink("lagomorph_mod.txt")
cat("
model{

#Priors
sigma.sigma ~ dunif(0,10) # overdispersion in sigma (transect-level)
tau.sigma <- pow(sigma.sigma,-2)
sigma.lambda ~ dunif(0,10) # overdispersion in lambda (transect-level)
tau.lambda <- pow(sigma.lambda,-2)
sigma.patch ~ dunif(0,10) # overdispersion in lambda (patch-level)
tau.patch <- pow(sigma.patch,-2)

# beta coefficients for transect-level covariates
for(i in 1:10){beta[i] ~ dnorm(0,0.001)}

# intercept for sigma
exp.mu.sigma ~ dunif(0,10) # for R. spinosus: exp.mu.sigma ~ dnorm(0,0.01)I(0,)
mu.sigma <- log(exp.mu.sigma)

# intercept and coefficients related to patch-level density
mu0 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)I(-20,20)
for(g in 1:10){gamma[g] ~ dnorm(0,0.001)}

C <- 100000 #these are for the 'ones-trick' in WinBUGS, see Chelgren, Shirk, and the BUGS manual
pi <- 3.14159

# Likelihood
# Patch-level model for mu
for (k in 1:5){        #loop over 5 survey occasions
    for(f in 1:n.patches){        #loop over 86 patches
        mu[f,k] <- mu0 + inprod(gamma[],Z[f,]) + e.mu <http://e.mu>[f,k]
        e.mu <http://e.mu>[f,k] ~ dnorm(0,tau.patch)I(-20,20) #random error
    } #f
    for (i in 1:transects){# loop through all 1051 transects
        # Transect-level model for lambda (expectation of abundance)
        lambda.model[i,k] <- mu[patch.id <http://patch.id>[i],k] + inprod(beta[],X[i,]) + e.lambda[i,k]
        e.lambda[i,k] ~ dnorm(0,tau.lambda)I(-20,20) #random error
        lambda[i,k] <- (L[i]*W*2)*exp(lambda.model[i,k])

        # the number present at transect i is Poisson distributed
        N[i,k] ~ dpois(lambda[i,k])

        # allow sigma (detection curve) to vary by transect
        log.sigma[i,k] <- mu.sigma + e.sigma[i,k]
        e.sigma[i,k] ~ dnorm(0,tau.sigma)I(-20,20)
        sigma[i,k] <- exp(log.sigma[i,k])

        # detection probability within the strip plot
        Pa[i,k] <- (1/W)*sqrt(2*pi)*sigma[i,k]*(phi(W/sigma[i,k])-0.5)
        Pa.x[i,k] <- max(0.001,min(Pa[i,k],0.999)) # bounds detection between 0.001 and 0.999

        # model the number observed given true abundance and detection probability
        n[i,k] ~ dbin(Pa.x[i,k],N[i,k])

        # Compute fit statistics
        eval[i,k] <- Pa.x[i,k]*N[i,k] # expected values
        E[i,k] <- pow((n[i,k]-eval[i,k]),2)/(eval[i,k]+0.5) # fit of observed data
        #n.new <http://n.new>[i,k] ~ dbin(Pa.x[i,k],N[i,k]) # replicate values
        #E.new[i,k] <- pow((n.new <http://n.new>[i,k]-eval[i,k]),2)/(eval[i,k]+0.5) # fit of replicate data
    } #i

    for (i in 1:transects1[k]){ #loop through transects having >= 1 detections
        for (j in 1:n[tran1_ik[i,k],k]) { #loop through all n[i] detections for transect i
            # likelihood of observed distances WITH truncation at T.
            Lik[tran1_ik[i,k],j,k] < -1/sigma[tran1_ik[i,k],k]*pow(2*pi,-0.5)*exp(-0.5*pow(y[tran1_ik[i,k],j,k]/sigma[tran1_ik[i,k],k],2))/(phi(T/sigma[tran1_ik[i,k],k])-0.5)

            # the following three lines implement the 'ones trick' (see the WinBUGS user manual)
            ones[tran1_ik[i,k],j,k] <- 1
            p[tran1_ik[i,k],j,k] <- Lik[tran1_ik[i,k],j,k] / C
            ones[tran1_ik[i,k],j,k] ~ dbern(p[tran1_ik[i,k],j,k])
        }   #j
    }  #i
}  #k

# calculate transect density (per ha) per sampling occasion
for (k in 1:5){
    for (i in 1:transects){
        dens.tran[i,k] <- (N[i,k]/(2*W*L[i]))*10000
    }  #i
}#k
} # end model
",fill=TRUE)
sink()

#MCMC settings
ni=500
nb=100
nthin=10
nc=2

#Initial values
Nst <- apply(n,c(1,2),max) +1
Nst[is.na <http://is.na>(Nst)] <- 1
inits <- function(){list(N=Nst, beta=runif(10,-1,1),gamma=runif(10,-1,1))}

#Bundle data
data1 <- list(y = y, n=n,transects=transects,transects1=transects1,tran1_ik=tran1_ik,
    n.patches=n.patches,patch.id <http://patch.id>=patch.id <http://patch.id>,Z=Z,X=X,L=L,W=W,T=T)

#Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("sigma","dens.tran")

#Call OpenBUGS from R
winbugs.out <- bugs(data1,inits,parameters,"lagomorph_mod.txt", n.thin=nthin,n.chains=nc, burnin=nb,n.iter=ni,debug=TRUE,DIC=FALSE,bugs.directory=bugs.dir)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lucretia,

I am currently having LOTS of problems with hierarchical distance sampling
models (with N-mixture models combined with distance sampling a la Chandler 2011 -
gdistsamp, Royle 2004) as well.
My problem is convergence of the availability intercept vs the lambda
intercept - these models are simply very slow and do not converge even after
120 000 iterations (like 36 hours on single CPU). My solution was to give up on
fitting those models and simply assume probability of availability being some fixed constant
(like pA = 0.9). Your problem might be different though. First of all, unless you using spatial autocorrelation
features of the GeoBUGS (spatial.exp or car.normal) I suggest you throw out
WinBUGS out of the Window and use JAGS instead. The problem of WinBUGS is
that those error messages will tell you nothing and are very hard to diagnose.
JAGS will give you much more friendly error output, which will help you find
the error.

Good luck

        Tomas

Hi Lucretia,

I agree that JAGS may work better for a number of reasons (try the jagsUI package).  My other suggestion is that you should simplify this model considerably and then build up.  Try models without any covariates and error terms to get a better feel for how everything works and make sure that the parameter and model specifications (particularly with regards to indexing) are correct.  It is tempting to throw a complex model at your data when you think it better captures the observational and ecological processes, but it can make troubleshooting very difficult!

You might also try setting all regression coefficients for covariates to have initial values of 0.  Technically you want the chains to start from different places to assess convergence, but with that many covariates, the initial values could suggest a parameter space that will cause computational errors.  Again though, if you incrementally add covariates you might more easily identify problems.

Hi all,

not much specific that I can add to the discussion but I want to wholeheartedly second what Dan says about starting with a simple model and then add in complexity. This alone is the most imoprtant general modeling tipp for BUGS (or indeed any complex statistical modeling), and by far. If you can't fit the simple model, you will never be able to fit the more complex models that you really want to go to. And if you have a more complex model that does not work, then the best advice is to "go back" to one that does, which always means, reduce complexity until you are at a model that does work and then build up again.

Hence, in summary, it's always best to start very simple and then add complexity incrementally.

Thanks, Dan, for bringing this up !

Regards  --   Marc

On Thursday, March 19, 2015 at 1:21:11 PM UTC-6, marc.kery wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> not much specific that I can add to the discussion but I want to wholeheartedly second what Dan says about starting with a simple model and then add in complexity. This alone is the most imoprtant general modeling tipp for BUGS (or indeed any complex statistical modeling), and by far. If you can't fit the simple model, you will never be able to fit the more complex models that you really want to go to. And if you have a more complex model that does not work, then the best advice is to "go back" to one that does, which always means, reduce complexity until you are at a model that does work and then build up again.
>
> Hence, in summary, it's always best to start very simple and then add complexity incrementally.
>
> Thanks, Dan, for bringing this up !
>
> Regards  --   Marc

Try models without any covariates and error terms to get a better feel for how everything works and make sure that the parameter and model specifications (particularly with regards to indexing) are correct.  It is tempting to throw a complex model at your data when you think it better captures the observational and ecological processes, but it can make troubleshooting very difficult!
>
> You might also try setting all regression coefficients for covariates to have initial values of 0.  Technically you want the chains to start from different places to assess convergence, but with that many covariates, the initial values could suggest a parameter space that will cause computational errors.  Again though, if you incrementally add covariates you might more easily identify problems.
